ety.text: From Middle English obgectyf, from Middle French objectif and its etymon Medieval Latin obiectīvus. By surface analysis, object + -ive.

senses.d: Of or relating to a material object, actual existence or reality.
Not influenced by the strong emotions or prejudices.
Based on observed facts; without purely subjective assessment.
Mind-independent
ex: The value of pedagogical material informed by objective methodological procedures developed in corpus linguistics is widely recognized.

senses.d: Of, or relating to a noun or pronoun used as the object of a verb.
ex: The objective complement in "She makes us angry" is the adjective "angry".

senses.d: Of, or relating to verbal conjugation that indicates the object (patient) of an action. (In linguistic descriptions of Tundra Nenets, among others.)
A material object that physically exists.
A goal that is striven for.
ex: The new imperative for investment is the Government's objective to secure carbon-neutral transport emissions by 2040.

senses.d: The objective case.
a noun or pronoun in the objective case.
The lens or lenses of a camera, microscope, or other optical device closest to the object being examined.

grp.label: not influenced by irrational emotions or personal prejudices
based on observed fact, evidence; unbiased

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin objectivus. See objet and -if.

From Middle French but (“mark, goal”), from Old French but (“aim, goal, end, target”), from Old French butte (“mound, knoll, target”), from Frankish *but (“stump, log”), or from Old Norse bútr (“log, stump, butt”); both from Proto-Germanic *buttaz (“end, piece”). Cognate with Old English butt (“tree stump”); see butt.

English object From Old French object, from Medieval Latin obiectum (“object”, literally “thrown against”), from obiectus, perfect passive participle of obiciō (“to throw against”), from ob- (“against”) + iaciō (“to throw”), as a calque of Ancient Greek ἀντικείμενον (antikeímenon).

senses.d: A thing that has physical existence but is not alive.
Objective; goal, end or purpose of something.
ex:
Money is an Object to you?
Money is an Object to me.

senses.d: The noun phrase which is an internal complement of a verb phrase or a prepositional phrase. In a verb phrase with a transitive action verb, it is typically the receiver of the action.
A person or thing toward which an emotion is directed.
ex: Mary Jane had been the object of Peter's affection for years.
The convertible, once the object of his desire, was now the object of his hatred.

senses.d: A cause for attention or concern.
ex: the object of a strongly worded censure
Money is no object to him.

senses.d: An instantiation of a class or structure.
An instance of one of the two kinds of entities that form a category, the other kind being the arrows (also called morphisms).
ex: Similarly, there is a category whose objects are groups and whose arrows are the homomorphisms from one group to another.

senses.d: Sight; show; appearance; aspect.
ex:
c. 1610s, George Chapman, Batrachomyomachia
He, advancing close / Up to the lake, past all the rest, arose / In glorious object.

senses.d: To disagree with or oppose something or someone; (especially in a Court of Law) to raise an objection.
ex: I object to the proposal to build a new airport terminal.
We strongly object to sending her to jail for ten years.

senses.d: To offer in opposition as a criminal charge or by way of accusation or reproach; to adduce as an objection or adverse reason.
ex: He 'gan to him object his heinous Crime,
There are others who will object the poverty of the nation.

senses.d: To set before or against; to bring into opposition; to oppose.
ex:
c. 1678, Richard Hooker, a sermon
some strong impediment or other objecting itself
Pallas to their eyes / The mist objected, and condens'd the skies.

grp.label: 2. the goal, end or purpose of something
4. person or thing to which an emotion is directed
5. object-oriented programming: instantiation of a class or structure

ety.text: From Middle French objection, from Old French objeccion, from Latin obiectio. Equivalent to object + -ion.

senses.d: The act of objecting.
ex: last-minute objection

senses.d: A statement expressing opposition, or a reason or cause for expressing opposition (generally followed by the adposition to).
ex: I have no objection to any person's religion.

senses.d: An official protest raised in a court of law during a legal trial over a violation of the rules of the court by the opposing party.
ex: Counsel for the property owner immediately raised an objection which was sustained following argument outside the presence of the jury.

senses.d: An assertion that a question or statement is in violation of the rules of the court.
ex: Objection! That is irrelevant to this case, Your Honor!

grp.label: official protest raised in a court of law
